prompt: Some people think it’s better to choose friends who always have the same opinions as them. Other people believe it’s good to have friends who sometimes disagree with them. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Choosing friends is an important part of personal development, and people often have different opinions about what makes a good friendship. Some individuals prefer friends who share the same opinions and values, while others believe that friendships are more beneficial when people sometimes disagree with each other. In my opinion, although having similar values can create harmony, friendships that include occasional disagreements are generally more valuable because they encourage personal growth and critical thinking.

On the one hand, people who prefer friends with similar opinions argue that such relationships are usually more stable and comfortable. When friends share the same beliefs about education, career goals, lifestyle, or social issues, they tend to experience fewer conflicts and misunderstandings. This can create a strong sense of trust and emotional support. For example, students who have similar academic ambitions often motivate each other to study consistently and achieve their goals. In difficult situations, friends with similar viewpoints may also provide advice that feels reassuring and familiar.

On the other hand, many people believe that friendships should not be based on complete agreement. Friends who occasionally disagree can introduce new perspectives and challenge assumptions that we may never question on our own. Constructive disagreement helps individuals develop critical thinking skills, become more open-minded, and make better decisions. For instance, I have experienced situations in which a friend disagreed with my career choices and suggested alternative options that I had not considered before. Although the conversation was initially uncomfortable, it helped me evaluate my decision more carefully and ultimately make a more informed choice.

I believe that the most meaningful friendships are those that combine mutual respect with honest disagreement. Constant agreement may sometimes limit personal growth because people remain within a narrow circle of ideas. In contrast, respectful discussions with friends who hold different opinions can broaden our understanding of the world and improve our communication skills. However, this does not mean that friends should disagree about everything; core values such as trust, kindness, and respect should still be shared.

In conclusion, while friendships based on similar opinions can provide comfort, stability, and emotional support, I believe that friendships that allow occasional disagreement are more beneficial. They promote critical thinking, open-mindedness, and personal development while still maintaining strong and supportive relationships when mutual respect is present.
